absent: Full layouts of event, context, PMU, attribute, and group tree structures beyond fields touched here.
Contracts of PMU callbacks for add, remove, start, stop, enable, disable, and filtering.
Properties of the clock source behind time stamps including units and wrap handling.
Admission and multiplexing policy for installing groups and flexible rotation.
Outer lock ordering and interrupt safety beyond the asserted context lock and noted guards.
Lifetime and reference rules for cgroup objects beyond connect and detach shown.
Meaning and full value set of event type flags and event state enumeration.
Behavior of time readers in non maskable interrupt context beyond the offset mechanism.

findings.text: Two globally visible PMU helpers manage a per CPU disable nesting count and forward only outermost transitions to underlying PMU callbacks, giving balanced disable and enable pairing for scheduling paths.
Time slot positions distinguish total time at zero from guest time at one for use when computing mediated virtual PMU adjustments.

Changing an event state does nothing when old and new states match, otherwise it refreshes own time accounting and, on a change of enabledness sign, sibling group time, then publishes the new state with ordered write semantics.

Iteration over PMU contexts skips entries with no cgroup events when cgroup filtering is requested, skips entries whose PMU lacks mediated virtual PMU capability when guest filtering is requested, and optionally restricts to one selected PMU.
Context disable and context enable each walk every retained PMU context and apply the matching per PMU operation, so context scheduling brackets hardware access with balanced nesting.

Time bookkeeping optionally advances accumulated time by elapsed wall time, stamps current time, and maintains an offset equal to accumulated minus stamp so readers can compute current time from ordered reads without locks.
When mediated guest support is loaded and an event excludes guest execution, current time is total offset minus guest offset; otherwise it is current time plus total offset.

An event with no cgroup always matches the current CPU; an event with a cgroup matches only when the CPU has an associated cgroup equal to or descending from the event cgroup, giving recursive membership.

CPU cgroup time updates walk from the current cgroup toward ancestors refreshing each level total time and, when mediated guest support is loaded, guest time, optionally clearing active markers on final teardown.
Event driven cgroup time refresh applies only to cgroup events with pinned state and only while the per CPU cgroup info for that event is marked active.

Context scheduling out and in plus context time refresh helpers require the context lock held by the caller, enforced by ownership assertions, because they mutate active flags, times, and group lists.
Establishing cgroup timestamps expects the context lock held and the CPU cgroup pinned, then stamps each ancestor level and publishes active state with release ordering for non guest paths.

Cgroup switching uses a scoped guard covering CPU and task contexts, rechecks CPU association after acquiring the lock to handle removal races, and brackets rescheduling with cgroup filtered disable and enable.
Growth of per CPU merge heaps for deeper cgroup nesting is protected by taking the per CPU context lock with interrupts disabled around the pointer swap and size update.

A time context carries accumulated time, last stamp, and derived offset; event contexts keep separate total and guest instances, and per CPU cgroup info keeps total time, guest time, and an active flag.

An event context tracks active flags, event and frequency and cgroup counts, optional task linkage, pinned and flexible group collections, and a list of PMU contexts; each PMU context links to its context and PMU and holds pinned and flexible active lists plus rotation and count state.

CPU scheduling state links a CPU event context, optional task context, optional current cgroup, and a reusable merge heap with capacity; group lookup keys combine CPU number, PMU identity, and cgroup identity.

Scheduling an event out applies only to active events, removes active tracking, marks the CPU slot vacant, and selects inactive as next state unless a pending disable was recorded, in which case it clears the pending flag, releases cgroup association, and selects off.

Context active flags track pinned, flexible, time, frozen, and guest kinds; sched out always refreshes time when set, preserves frozen time across out for later cleanup, and guest transitions add extra timestamp and barrier steps before and after flag changes.

Per CPU cgroup active markers are published with release semantics when timestamps are established and cleared with release semantics on final updates, while readers use acquire semantics to choose between interpolating running time and returning frozen time.

Scheduling a context in starts time if needed, marks requested kinds active, attaches task context on first activation, then installs pinned groups before flexible groups across matching PMU contexts.

Group installation merges sorted group streams by CPU, PMU, and cgroup ancestry with a min heap sized for per CPU plus nested cgroup iterators, applies PMU filtering and task linkage, then invokes a caller callback per group until exhaustion or early stop.
Group and event scheduling paths require the target PMU already disabled through the nesting count and assert this precondition, so callers must bracket list walks that change hardware state.
Scheduling out an empty context warns if it remains marked active or retains task association, signaling a lifecycle or reference imbalance rather than silently succeeding.
Cgroup heap sizing grows each per CPU heap to one plus nesting depth and reports allocation failure without disturbing existing storage, so deep hierarchies need proportional merge capacity.

Attaching an event to a cgroup file needs a valid descriptor and online subsystem state plus sufficient heap capacity, and rejects groups whose members target different cgroups because a task belongs to one perf cgroup at a time.
Without cgroup perf support, timestamping, time propagation, event disable, detach, and cgroup extraction become empty operations that preserve call structure with no state effect.

Scheduling out adjusts active CPU count only for non software events, adjusts frequency counts only when both frequency flag and sample rate are set, and clears exclusivity when the event was exclusive or no active events remain.
Task bound PMU contexts are recorded in per CPU PMU state on first scheduling use with a conflict warning, and that linkage is cleared when the owning task context loses all active kinds.
Scheduling a group out is a no operation unless the leader is active; otherwise the leader is removed first and then each sibling in turn.

Context time refresh runs only while time is active and is skipped while frozen; normal updates advance total and guest times when mediated support is loaded, while guest transitions use separate guest stamping.
